Growing Up Yazidi: Family, Faith, and the Edges of the World.
Picture this—rolling hills in northern Iraq, where life moves to rhythms that haven’t really changed in generations. For a Yazidi child, the world feels small, safe, and full of meaning. Mornings start with sunlight spilling over the fields, and every evening winds down with the warmth of family voices, sharing a simple meal together.
There’s a comfort in knowing everyone’s story—neighbors who look out for each other, and a quiet pride in belonging to a people who’ve weathered centuries of hardship. It’s the kind of place where safety comes from community, from feeling seen and understood by those around you.
For a young Yazidi girl, tradition is everything. She learns by watching her mother prepare special dishes for festivals, listens to elders share stories about times when their people faced terrible danger, and helps her siblings with chores that keep their home running. The Yazidi faith isn’t just a set of beliefs—it’s woven into daily life, wrapped up in customs, sacred places, and rituals that mark every season and milestone. There’s a deep respect for the land, for ancestors who came before, and for ceremonies that connect everyone to their roots.
But even in this close-knit world, there’s a sense that danger sometimes lurks just beyond the edges. Being Yazidi means belonging to a small minority—one that’s often misunderstood or even targeted by outsiders. Parents worry about their kids, and stories of past violence hang in the air, shaping how the community views the wider world. Still, hope finds a way. Many Yazidi families see education as a lifeline—a way for their children to dream of a future with more choices than their parents ever had. They make real sacrifices to send their kids to school, holding onto the hope that learning can open doors that have always been closed.
Imagine a quiet afternoon, where a girl sits in the shade of a fig tree with her siblings, listening as their mother talks about the importance of dignity and kindness. The conversation drifts from family history to the struggles of being Yazidi in a world that doesn’t always understand. You can hear the strength in her mother’s voice, but there’s worry too—she wants her children to be proud, but she knows that showing pride can be dangerous when others don’t accept your differences.
As time passes, the world outside the village starts to feel a little closer. News of unrest in distant cities trickles in—sometimes from travelers, sometimes as whispers in the marketplace. Yet, most days still look much the same: there are fields to work, prayers to say, and celebrations to prepare for. Family ties stay strong, and community brings comfort, even when the world feels uncertain.
It’s easy to forget just how precious the small freedoms of childhood can be—the laughter shared with friends, the safety of a loving home, the simple belief that you’ll always have a place to belong. For Yazidi families, these moments are treasured, precisely because they know how fragile they are. There’s always a quiet awareness that everything could change in a heartbeat.
And yet, hope endures. In those quiet moments before drifting off to sleep, the girl dreams of a future where her people can live without fear, where their traditions are honored, and where every child grows up believing that their story truly matters.
